posts.content_md:
Have you any experience with either 01 or 03, or are you simply making opinions from data on the web site. Surely even you agree that experience is far more valuable.

I did not say the two were identical. Perhaps however, the idealised parameters for the two films on the website do not take mitigating circumstances into account., such variations in temperature. Again, I assume you have no actual experience. I think anyone with experience on these films would agree that grain size alone is not the complete criterion for exposure. However, since you seem to be making these comments purely on a theoretical basis, you mention "resolving power". Which "resolving power" exactly? Are you referring to the resolving power of the fringes or the resolving power of the grains? If the latter, are we talking the diffraction limited Airy radius or Rayleigh criteria. If either, perhaps we could have the diffraction pattern around the grain. I assume you'd be using the Helmholtz-Kirchgoff integral, although it should be interesting trying to derive the integral for a volume object. Of course, you could always alter the Green's function from

G = exp(ikr_01)/r_01

to take the volume effect into consideration. Perhaps

G = cos(S.r)exp(ikr_01)/r_01

Thus introducing a sort of "obliquity factor". However you do need to take into account that the grain size is smaller than lambda. so I'm not sure what your boundary conditions would be. I don't think that the Kirchoff boundary condition:

U(P_0) = 1/(4pi)(SS(dU/dn*G - U*dg/dn)ds (where SS represents the integral over the surface)

 would be quite adequate unless again you also altered the Green's function. Perhaps you could recover the boundary condition by an appropriate choice of Green's function that satisfy both criteria? 

You might see that actual experience is a somewhat easier path then your theoretical approach.

It's possible that you mean by "resolving power" the resolution of the Fourier fringes. In this case, since the actual fringes are "quantised", or, at least, particulate, you'd need to use some integral terms and some summations. This, of course, would depend more on the grain density than the actual size of which we have no figures. Again, I submit that practical experience is a better criterion. Prhaps you could relate yours rather than appeal to arcane theoretical studies.... 

As for every setup being different, if the object changes, the energy profile, and the beam ratio changes. You say you shot for 20 hours straight - for roughly the same object. I shot for four years straight at ABNH and still maintain that every shot is different. They were the same at ABNH because all the objects were roughly the same. If the object changes then the beam profile changes, the ratio changes, the polarisation, or lack thereof, changes, the aestheticism changes. I think that most practical holographers will bear me out about test shots. Again, it's all a matter of experience.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:1c0230894d="BobH"][quote:1c0230894d]You can't measure the de of a display hologram, since a display hologram is photometric, not radiometric. [/quote:1c0230894d]

What if I put a reflection hologram in the collimated beam of a spectrometer, at the reference angle, and measure the depletion of the beam. Wouldn't that give me the DE?[/quote:1c0230894d]

It would give you the radiometric efficency with respect to the measured output of the (coherent) laser source. It would not give you the "brightness" of the hologram wrt the white light source reconstructing the hologram. I have several of Don's old reflection master upstairs. Don made them incredibly narrow band in DCG at 488 so they're practically invisible in white light even though they very bright under the laser. If by "de", you mean the popular concept of how "bright" a hologram is, then Don's holograms are very weak. If by de you mean the ratio of input light to output light at a particular wavelength measured in W/sq m, then you need to specify the wavelength. Due to various phenomena such as noise, scattering etc, I suspect that reconstructing a particularly broad band reflection hologram under different laser frequencies will give you different values for the de. Of course if the hologram is narrow band, you won't be able to measure the de under different laser frequencies and so the question of de vs lambda becomes moot. But the principle remains, the "brightness" of a hologram is determined by photopic considerations as well as the colour temperature of the reconstruction source (which would also contribute to the photopic "brightness"), while the ratio I_h/I_O where I_h is the measured intensity of the holographic image and I_O is the measured intensity of the laser, is esentially radiometric. Of course, you also have the spatial frequency range of a display hologram (I mean here the spatial frequencies of the image - the FT of the holographic image - not the spatial frequency of the fringe pattern) which would also come into the radiometric de but not the photometric one.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
> If by de you mean the ratio of input light to output light at a particular wavelength measured in W/sq m, then you need to specify the wavelength.

This is indeed what I mean by "DE". If I illuminate a reflection hologram at its best reconstruction angle with the collimated white light beam of an Ocean Optics spectrometer system (detecting the transmitted beam), I'll get a plot of percent transmission vs wavelength. The system is calibrated with a piece of plain glass to remove the effect of reflections. The baseline of the plot shows me the effect of the scatter and/or absorption. The curve shows the DE as a function of wavelength, at the position on the display hologram I'm probing. 

My point is that you *can* measure the DE of a display hologram. I'd also suggest that probing a display hologram with a laser having the same color as the hologram will also yield its DE. I wouldn't recommend it , however, since the beam has a high probability of "printing out" a dark spot on the image!

[/quote:acfa16bf10]

Yes, that's true.. But in terms of a display reflection hologram, what are the components of the "white light"? If you put in a reflection hologram designed to reconstruct at, say 420nm, you may get an exceptionally good OD of let's say 3 or 4. Make the same hologram with the same OD but peaked at 550nm. Both holograms have the same OD, 3, however, I'd suggest that the one reconstructing at 550nm is going to appear a lot brighter with a white light source than the one at 420nm. So, you're right that the "de" is a measurable quantity, but is it a fair characteristic in terms of the visual brightness of the reflection hologram? If you show the (OD = 3.0) hologram at 550 and the same one at the same OD reconstructing at 420 to a lay person, which one would he/she say is "brighter"? If you then explain that the " holographic efficency" is the same, you might get a funny look! My point is: what exactly is meant by "de" in terms of a hologram that's designed to be viewed by the human visual system? You can, of course, define and measure a radiometric "de", but is this sensible in terms of the use of the hologram as an object designed to be appreciated for it's visual impact?
